progressions.name: I–IV–V–I
progressions.explanation: The three primary chords. I is home, IV leaves it gently, V creates the strongest pull back to I.
progressions.practice: Play each chord with the left-hand root and a close right-hand triad. Say the chord names aloud as you change.

progressions.name: I–V–vi–IV
progressions.explanation: The most common modern pop and worship loop. The minor vi chord adds a touch of sadness before IV lifts it again.
progressions.practice: Keep the right hand in one small area and move to the nearest inversion each time.

progressions.name: I–vi–IV–V
progressions.explanation: The 1950s progression: tonic, its relative minor, subdominant, dominant.
progressions.practice: Play in steady quarter notes, then try one chord per bar.

progressions.name: vi–IV–I–V
progressions.explanation: The same four chords as I–V–vi–IV starting on the minor chord, which gives a more reflective feel.
progressions.practice: Compare it with I–V–vi–IV: same chords, different starting point.

progressions.name: I–iii–IV–V
progressions.explanation: A rising gospel build: each chord climbs one step, with iii acting as a soft tonic substitute.
progressions.practice: Voice the right hand so the top note climbs by step: E, G, A, B.

progressions.name: ii–V–I
progressions.explanation: The core jazz cadence. ii prepares V, V resolves to I; the root moves down a fifth each time.
progressions.practice: Voice it with guide tones: the 7th of each chord falls to the 3rd of the next.

progressions.name: ii–V–I–vi
progressions.explanation: ii–V–I followed by vi, which keeps the harmony moving instead of coming to rest.
progressions.practice: Notice the root keeps falling a fifth: D, G, C, then up a third to A.

progressions.name: I–vi–ii–V
progressions.explanation: The classic turnaround. The roots descend a fifth each time from vi, so it loops naturally back to I.
progressions.practice: Play it as a loop, two bars per chord pair, until the change back to I feels automatic.

progressions.name: iii–vi–ii–V
progressions.explanation: A chain of falling fifths leading into V. Often used to reach the tonic from the third degree.
progressions.practice: Practise it before a final I so you hear what the chain is aiming at.

progressions.name: 12-bar blues
progressions.explanation: Twelve bars built on I, IV and V. All three chords are usually played as dominant sevenths. The last V is the turnaround.
progressions.practice: Count the bars aloud. Learn the shape first (4 bars I, 2 bars IV, 2 bars I, then V IV I V).

progressions.name: i–iv–V–i
progressions.explanation: The minor key's basic cadence. V is borrowed from the harmonic minor scale (it has the raised seventh) so it pulls strongly to i.
progressions.practice: Play the V chord and notice the raised seventh scale degree resolving up to the tonic.

progressions.name: ii°–V–i
progressions.explanation: The minor-key version of ii–V–I. The ii chord is half-diminished and V is a dominant seventh.
progressions.practice: Compare with the major ii–V–I; only the first and last chords change quality.

progressions.name: i–VII–VI–V
progressions.explanation: The Andalusian cadence: a descending line (A G F E in A minor) ending on the dominant.
progressions.practice: Listen for the stepwise descending bass line.

progressions.name: i–VI–III–VII
progressions.explanation: A common minor-key pop loop that moves through the relative major (III).
progressions.practice: Keep the same hand shape and slide it to each new chord.

progressions.name: I–V7/ii–ii–V
progressions.explanation: A turnaround where the vi chord is replaced by V7 of ii, so the line leads strongly into ii.
progressions.practice: Hear how the third of the A7 (C#) is the only note outside the key.

progressions.name: I–vii°7/ii–ii–V
progressions.explanation: A passing diminished chord a half step below ii connects I to ii with a chromatic bass line.
progressions.practice: Play the bass line C, C#, D, G and listen to the chromatic step.

progressions.name: iv–bVII7–I
progressions.explanation: The backdoor ii–V: borrowed iv and bVII7 resolve down to I instead of the usual V.
progressions.practice: Compare how bVII7 resolves with the more familiar V7.

progressions.name: Gospel walk-up
progressions.explanation: A walking bass line from I up to V through chord inversions and a passing diminished chord, a staple of gospel.
progressions.practice: Play the bass line alone first: C, E, F, F#, G. Then add the right-hand chords.
